name: Evening hot shower / bath

lead: A warm shower or bath in the evening is used to ease into sleep. The idea is that it relaxes you and helps you fall asleep faster, so you wake up looking more rested and fresher.

Proponents say the body cools after the bath and the drop in core temperature signals sleep. This claim circulates in sleep and looksmaxxing communities; the Wikipedia articles on sleep onset and hot tubs, the pages reviewed, do not cover it, and no study was found testing it for appearance.

paras: People take a warm shower or bath roughly an hour or so before bed as part of a wind-down routine, followed by a cool, dark bedroom.
Very hot water can cause drowsiness or dizziness; the hot tub article treats drowsiness in water above body temperature as a drowning risk.

angle.text: A warm shower or bath before bed helps you fall asleep faster as your body cools afterward, and better sleep supports a rested, fresher look. Evidence for the routine is thin.

lead: The evening hot shower or bath is a pre-bed routine of washing in warm or hot water shortly before sleep. Proponents say it promotes sleep onset by relaxing the body and, as the body cools afterward, lowering core temperature. For looks, the appeal is the chain from better sleep to a more rested appearance: Wikipedia's sleep deprivation article lists periorbital puffiness, the so-called eye bags, among the effects of too little sleep.[1]

The routine is circulated in sleep and looksmaxxing communities as a simple wind-down habit. Sleep-hygiene guidance in general recommends relaxing activities before bedtime, a regular schedule and a cool, dark, quiet sleeping space, though the Wikipedia article on sleep hygiene does not specifically mention warm baths.[2]

Source material for this entry is thin: the Wikipedia pages on hot tubs and sleep hygiene do not cover the bath-before-bed claim, and the hot tub article notes that sitting in water above normal body temperature can cause drowsiness, which it presents as a drowning risk. Training-forum posters also mention hot baths and showers after exercise in their logs.
infobox: Hot water can cause drowsiness or dizziness

paras: Practitioners take a warm or hot shower or bath in the evening before bed. Proponents attribute faster sleep onset to relaxation and to the temperature change afterward, as the body loses the heat it gained.

Wikipedia's sleep deprivation article lists periorbital puffiness, commonly called bags under the eyes, among the effects of sleep loss.[1] Practitioners who adopt the evening bath as a sleep aid generally frame it as one part of a wider routine of regular sleep timing and a calm, cool bedroom of the kind sleep-hygiene guidance describes.[2]

The hot tub article notes that sitting in water above normal body temperatures can cause drowsiness, which is a drowning risk in that setting. The site note for this entry also lists dizziness as a possible effect of very hot water.
No studies found in the sources reviewed for this entry on evening showers or baths and sleep onset.

lore.intro: A warm evening shower or bath is discussed as a simple sleep aid and wind-down habit.[2]
